Learning Objectives
Discuss arthroplasty treatment options for the management of femoral neck fractures.
Describe the indications and contraindications for hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty.
List the advantages and disadvantages of hemiarthroplasty versus total hip arthroplasty..
Review the outcomes of hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty.

Background
Hip fractures are a substantial cause of morbidity and mortality and represent a major
healthcare burden (Resource 1).1 They are a top-10 cause of disability in adults.2 Each
year, 4.5 million individuals worldwide are disabled from a hip fracture.3,4 Because of an
aging population, the incidence of hip fractures is increasing. By the year 2050, more
than six million hip fractures will occur worldwide each year and approximately one-half
of hip fractures will involve the femoral neck.5 Risk factors for femoral neck fractures
include but are not limited to female sex, Caucasian race, and advanced age.
Patients with an unmanaged hip fracture are at risk for cardiovascular, pulmonary,
thrombotic, infectious, and bleeding complications, as well as death.3 Therefore, prompt
surgical management is recommended.3 Despite surgical management, the 1-year
mortality rate has been reported to be as high as 36%.3,6
The type of surgical treatment option for the management of femoral neck fractures is
controversial and usually is based on patient factors and fracture pattern (Resource 2).
Patient factors include age, functional capabilities, and comorbidities. The vascularity of
the femoral head is at risk in patients with a displaced femoral neck fracture. Patients
with such a fracture pattern have an increased risk for osteonecrosis of the femoral
head and fracture nonunion.7 Therefore, displaced femoral neck fractures are
commonly managed via hemiarthroplasty (Figures 1 and 2) or total hip arthroplasty
(THA; Figure 3).8 Whether hemiarthroplasty or THA is optimal remains a subject of
debate.1 Recent literature suggests THA results in better functional outcomes but is
associated with increased rates of dislocation in the initial postoperative period. In the
long-term, THA is not associated with higher dislocation rates and, therefore, may be
superior to hemiarthroplasty because of enhanced pain control.8

Hemiarthroplasty Versus THA
Indications
Indications for hip arthroplasty include Garden (displaced) type III and type IV femoral neck
fractures.
Most hemiarthroplasty or THA procedures can be performed to manage femoral neck
fractures.
Hemiarthroplasty often is useful in frail, elderly patients.
Many surgeons prefer THA, especially in patients with preexisting hip arthritis.


Indications
The ultimate goals of management are to minimize patient discomfort, restore and
attain the closest possible native hip function, and allow for early mobilization. Femoral
head vascularity is at risk in patients with a displaced femoral neck fracture. The medial
femoral circumflex artery is a major contributor to the blood supply to the femoral head.
Less contribution is from the lateral femoral circumflex artery and the inferior gluteal
artery. Patients with a displaced femoral neck fracture have a substantial risk of
osteonecrosis of the femoral head and fracture nonunion.7 Given these risks, femoral
neck fractures are commonly managed via hemiarthroplasty or THA.8 Management is
based on patient factors and radiographic fracture patterns. Patient factors include
patient age, activity level, comorbidities, and estimated survival.
Indications for arthroplasty include Garden type III femoral neck fractures (complete
fracture with partial displacement, often with varus angulation) and Garden type IV
femoral neck fractures (complete fracture with total displacement). The recommended
treatment option for Garden type I femoral neck fractures (incomplete fracture with
valgus impaction) and Garden type II femoral neck fractures (complete fracture,
nondisplaced) usually is open reduction and internal fixation with the use of screws.
THA has been advocated in patients with more mobility.1 THA has been suggested to
result in improved clinical outcomes in this patient population.1 Superior outcomes have
been reported after THA compared with hemiarthroplasty.8 Patients who underwent
THA had less pain and better clinical scores, especially at short-term follow-up.9 Patients
who are independently mobile and have no cognitive impairment or major medical
comorbidities should undergo THA. Independent ambulators with mobility limited to the
house or only short distances outside of the home should undergo hemiarthroplasty.
Patients with cognitive impairment, with poor mobility, who are in institutionalized care,
or with major medical comorbidities should undergo hemiarthroplasty or, occasionally,
not undergo arthroplasty.
Bhandari et al2 reported that the type of arthroplasty had no considerable effect on the
risk of unplanned secondary hip procedures within 2 years. In this trial, 57 of 718

patients (7.9%) who underwent THA required a secondary procedure within 2 years,
whereas 60 of 723 patients (8.3%) who underwent hemiarthroplasty required a
secondary procedure within 2 years (hazard ratio [HR], 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI]
0.64 to 1.40; P = 0.79).2 This corroborates the findings of other studies. A large
multicenter trial in Scotland that included 298 patients with a femoral neck fracture
demonstrated no considerable difference in the incidence of secondary hip procedures
at 24 months (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.24 to 2.81; P = 0.74).10 A larger analysis from the
Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry that included
17,985 femoral neck fractures managed over a period of 16 years suggested that THA
and hemiarthroplasty were associated with similar incidences of revision procedures
within 10 years (HR, 1.13; 95% CI, 0.95 to 1.33; P = 0.16).11
Studies suggest that the dislocation rates between the THA and hemiarthroplasty are not
significantly different after 4 years (P = 0.13).8 This suggests that an estimated patient
survival of 4 years or more is an indication for the selection of THA over
hemiarthroplasty. This also suggests that THA is indicated in all patients younger 80
years.8 Therefore, hemiarthroplasty may be indicated in patients older than 80 years or
who have a life expectancy of less than 4 years THA. The selection between THA or
hemiarthroplasty for a displaced femoral neck fracture should be based on each
patient’s overall health, activity level, and expectations, as well as the presence of
arthritis.
Contraindications
Elderly patients who are not physically fit enough to undergo arthroplasty
Contraindications to hemiarthroplasty include preexisting disease of the acetabulum.
Septic arthritis
Pregnancy

Contraindications for the management of hip fractures, specifically femoral neck
fractures, via arthroplasty include patients at high medical risk for surgical treatment.12
This also may be extended to patients who are demented, nonambulatory, or in minimal
pain.
Potential contraindications to hemiarthroplasty include patients younger than 80 years
or who have a life expectancy or more than 4 years. This patient population may achieve
better outcomes with THA. Patients with preexisting disease of the acetabulum also
should undergo a THA.
Potential contraindications to THA include patients older than 80 years who have a life
expectancy of less than 4 years. This patient population may achieve better outcomes
with hemiarthroplasty. Other contraindications to THA are household ambulators or
patients who can only ambulate for a short distance outside of the home. Any patient
with cognitive impairment, with poor mobility, who is in institutional care, or with major
medical comorbidities may have equivalent function with hemiarthroplasty.
Complications
Complications of femoral neck fractures include osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
Complications of hemiarthroplasty include acetabular erosion.
Complications of hemiarthroplasty and THA include dislocation.
Most conversions from hemiarthroplasty to THA are because of loosening or erosion of the
cartilage in the acetabulum.

Complications
Femoral neck fractures managed via internal fixation are associated with high
complication rates.8 Common complications include osteonecrosis of the femoral head,
the incidence of which increases with fracture severity and displacement; nonunion; and
hardware failure. This is a reason that most patients undergo THA or hemiarthroplasty.

In patients who initially underwent hemiarthroplasty, complications, such as acetabular
erosion, necessitate conversion to THA.12 Most conversions from hemiarthroplasty to
THA are performed because of hardware loosening and acetabular erosion (Resource 3).
A meta-analysis of 17 studies that included 1,364 patients reported no significant
difference in the rate of mortality or postoperative infection between patients who
underwent hemiarthroplasty versus THA (P = 0.89);8 however, an overall significant
increase in dislocation rate was reported in the patients who underwent THA (P <
0.0001).8 In a sub-analysis of patients with a follow-up period of 4 years or more, no
significant difference was noted in the dislocation rates between THA and
hemiarthroplasty (P = 0.13). Therefore, THA should be strongly considered in patients
with a life expectancy of 4 years or more.8
Bhandari et al2 noted that patients who underwent THA had a slightly increased
incidence of serious adverse events; however, no significant differences in mortality
were reported between patients who underwent THA versus hemiarthroplasty (14.3% in
THA group and 13.1% in hemiarthroplasty group; P = 0.48).2 Serious adverse events
occurred in 300 of 718 patients (41.8%) in the THA group and in 265 of 723 patients
(36.7%) in the hemiarthroplasty group (HR, 1.16; 99% CI, 0.90 to 1.51).2 Hip instability or
dislocation occurred in 34 of the THA patients (4.7%) and 17 of the hemiarthroplasty
patients (2.4%) (HR, 2.00; 95% CI, 0.97 to 4.09).2 A pooled estimate from randomized,
controlled trials suggested a 2.5 times greater risk of dislocation after THA compared
with hemiarthroplasty (9% versus 3%; relative risk, 2.53; 95% CI, 1.05 to 6.10).12
Using the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program
database, a 2020 study compared the trends of complication rates in 16,213 patients 50
years or older with a femoral neck fracture who underwent hemiarthroplasty or THA.1
No statistically significant difference in transfusion rates was reported between
hemiarthroplasty and THA based on the most recent years studied (2016 to 2017; P =
0.146);1 however, a significant increase in transfusion rates was reported with THA
compared with hemiarthroplasty between 2013 and 2015 (mean = 0.21 versus 0.19; P =
0.002) and 2010 and 2012 (mean = 0.34 versus 0.28; P = 0.001).1 Surgical times were
always significantly longer for THA (P < 0.001); however, a nonsignificant trend of

septic shock, acute renal failure, pulmonary embolism, requirement of a ventilator for
more than 48 hours, unplanned intubation, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, stroke
with neurologic deficit, and mortality within 30 days of the surgical procedure. Minor
complications analyzed included urinary tract infection, pneumonia, superficial surgical
site infection, wound dehiscence, progressive renal insufficiency, deep wound infection,
and deep vein thrombosis. No differences in major or minor complications were
reported in patients who underwent THA versus hemiarthroplasty. The authors also did
not note any differences in 30-day hospital readmission rates.1
Outcomes
Hemiarthroplasty is associated with lower initial dislocation rates and costs and less blood
loss.
THA result in better functional outcomes.

Outcomes
Hemiarthroplasty has been suggested to be a simpler procedure compared with THA.
Hemiarthroplasty is associated with lower initial costs and decreased blood loss.10
Hemiarthroplasty also is associated with lower early dislocation rates compared with
THA, possibly because of the decreased complexity of the surgical procedure; however,
THA is associated with better patient satisfaction scores and functional outcome scores.8
In addition, patients treated via hemiarthroplasty have an increased risk of revision
surgery.
Bhandari et al2 reported better functional outcomes during a 2-year period in patients
treated via THA versus hemiarthroplasty. Patients who underwent THA had better
function as measured by the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis
Index (WOMAC) total score (mean difference, -6.37; 99% CI, -9.18 to -3.56), WOMAC pain
score (mean difference, -0.93; 99% CI, -1.42 to -0.44), WOMAC stiffness score (mean
